title: The Standard Model of Particle Physics
seo_title: Year 12 Physics: The Standard Model Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Fundamental particles: six quarks and six leptons; hadrons (baryons and mesons); the four fundamental forces and their exchange particles; antimatter and annihilation; conservation of charge, baryon number and lepton number; particle accelerators and evidence for the Big Bang. (Senior Secondary Physics, Unit 4: Revolutions in modern physics)
meta_desc: Free Year 12 Physics worksheets on the Standard Model: quarks, leptons, baryons, mesons, exchange particles, the Higgs boson, antimatter, conservation laws and particle accelerators. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Matter = quarks + leptons; forces = exchange bosons.
key_sub: Charge, baryon number and lepton number are always conserved.
body_html:
How to think about it

The Standard Model describes matter with six quarks (up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom) and six leptons (electron, muon, tau and their neutrinos). Quarks combine into hadrons: baryons (three quarks: proton uud, neutron udd) and mesons (a quark and an antiquark).

Forces are carried by exchange bosons: photons (electromagnetic), gluons (strong), W and Z bosons (weak). The Higgs boson gives some particles mass. Every particle has an antiparticle; they annihilate into energy. Reactions must conserve charge, baryon number and lepton number.

Example

Charge of uud?

+2/3 + 2/3 − 1/3

Answer: +1 (a proton)

Example

Is p → n + e⁺ + ν possible for a free proton?

charge, baryon and lepton numbers balance

but the neutron has more mass

Answer: not for a free proton (energy)

Common mistakes

  • Thinking protons and neutrons are fundamental particles.
  • Calling a meson a baryon.
  • Saying gravity is carried by a detected particle in the Standard Model.

faq.q: Why is the Higgs boson important?
faq.a: Its field gives mass to the W and Z bosons and to the quarks and leptons; finding it at CERN in 2012 completed the Standard Model.

faq.q: What does the Standard Model not explain?
faq.a: Gravity, dark matter, dark energy and why there is more matter than antimatter.

items.q: Which particle is the only stable baryon?
items.e: A free neutron decays with a half-life of about 10 minutes.

items.q: What is a proton made of?
c: two up quarks and one down quark (uud)
one up and two down quarks

items.q: Which quantity is always conserved in particle interactions?
c: charge (also baryon number and lepton number)
items.e: Use conservation laws to check if a reaction is possible.

items.q: Which particle is a lepton?
items.e: Leptons do not feel the strong force.

items.q: How many gamma photons are usually produced when an electron and a positron annihilate at rest?
c: three, all in the same direction

items.q: What does a kaon usually decay into?
items.e: Kaons decay by the weak interaction into pions (or muons).

items.q: What is a neutrino?
c: a lepton with no charge and a very small mass that hardly interacts with matter
items.e: Trillions pass through you every second from the Sun.

items.q: Which exchange particle is involved in electron capture?
items.e: p + e⁻ → n + νₑ; a u quark becomes a d quark.

items.q: In a fluorescent tube, what makes the coating glow?
c: ultraviolet photons from the mercury vapour
items.e: Excited mercury atoms emit UV, which the coating absorbs and re-emits as visible light.

items.q: Which quantity is NOT always conserved in particle interactions?
items.e: Strangeness can change by ±1 in weak interactions.

items.q: Which particles carry the weak force?
items.e: The weak force causes beta decay.

items.q: In beta-minus decay, a down quark changes into which quark?
c: an up quark, emitting a W⁻ boson that decays to an electron and an antineutrino

items.q: Is the decay n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ (antineutrino) allowed?
c: no: lepton number is not conserved
yes: charge, baryon number and lepton number are all conserved
no: baryon number is not conserved

items.q: What is the charge of an up quark?
In β⁺ decay, which particles are emitted?
c: a positron and an electron neutrino

items.q: A π⁺ meson is made of which quarks?
items.e: Mesons are a quark and an antiquark: ⅔ + ⅓ = +1.

items.q: What is a meson?
c: a particle made of three quarks
a hadron made of a quark and an antiquark, such as a pion

items.q: Which observation is evidence that light behaves as particles?
items.e: Emission is instant and depends on frequency, not intensity.

items.q: What happens when a particle meets its antiparticle?
c: they annihilate, turning their mass into energy such as gamma photons
items.e: PET scans detect annihilation gamma rays.

items.q: Which particle is a meson?
items.e: Mesons are a quark–antiquark pair: pions and kaons.

c: A faint microwave glow comes evenly from every direction in the sky.
Almost every distant galaxy's light is redshifted.
About 75% of normal matter is hydrogen and about 25% is helium.
Very distant galaxies look younger and less developed.
